newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria sees more oil imports with refineries down.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria sees more oil imports with refineries down.

text.p: No end is in sight to fuel imports for oil producer Nigeria whose refineries badly need maintenance, while government ministries are squabbling over how to pay for repairs, officials said on Thursday.

Officials at state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) said it was certain that imports would have to continue after September, when a scheduled 33 cargoes of emergency fuel shipments are due to end.

"We have made representation to the government for the extension of fuel imports until the refineries are back," said a spokesman for NNPC's subsidiary, the Pipelines and Products Marketing Company, which handles both refineries and imports.
"We don't see the rehabilitation exercise completed by the end of September," the spokesman said.

Although Nigeria pumps over two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude, the poor condition of refineries, working well below their 445,000 bpd capacity, ensures sporadic and paralysing fuel shortages.
Months of scarcity have eased in the commercial capital Lagos, but in many parts of the country an inadequate distribution system not built to cope with imports, means that shortages persist.

Petroleum ministry officials say $200 million for repairs to at least some of four ailing refineries has been approved, but it has not been released and petroleum and finance ministries are at loggerheads over who gets the money.

"We are all ready to go, and NNPC has put everything in place. It is ridiculous that people should now go short of fuel because one ministry wants to take over the work of another," said a senior official at the petroleum ministry.
In the long term most industry analysts say the only solution is to put Nigeria's refineries in private hands.
"The fact that the petroleum products market has remained largely regulated is responsible for the crisis in the industry now...
"The way forward is through privatisation," said Joe Nwokedi, spokesman for a group of oil marketing companies recently.

Fixed fuel prices mean the refineries currently get only two naira ($0.024) for every litre they refine, way below world levels and nowhere near enough to pay for maintenance without running to government.

But even given a domestic market of over 100 million people in Africa's most populous nation, industry analysts say that privatised refineries would themselves have a battle to survive with shrinking margins elsewhere in the world.
And privatisation is an awkward subject, with vested interests are closely linked to the state-run bodies.
Business and the World Bank were both disappointed when military ruler General Sani Abacha shied away from privatisation in his 1997 budget in favour of further study.

International lenders and local economists push further liberalisation as one way to help Nigeria emerge from recession which has persisted since political chaos followed the annulment of 1993 elections by a previous military government.
